title: Korea: Traditional Liquors under the Liquor Tax Act (주세법)
attribution: Korea's Liquor Tax Act (주세법) defines its traditional drinks by production method and ingredient. The core split is between takju (unrefined, cloudy), yakju/cheongju (refined, clear) and soju (distilled), all built on the same nuruk-fermented rice base. Alongside the tax categories sit the government-designated Important Intangible Cultural Property folk liquors. Figures are typical commercial values; the category definitions are the legally meaningful part.

styles.name: Makgeolli / Takju (막걸리 / 濁酒)
styles.impression: Milky, lightly sparkling, sweet-tart and cloudy — Korea's oldest and most democratic drink, traditionally the farmer's brew.
styles.comments: Takju means 'cloudy liquor'. Unfiltered and often bottled live, so it keeps fermenting — modern bottles vent CO2. A carbonated, slightly effervescent farmhouse drink.
styles.ingredients: Steamed rice fermented with nuruk (a wild wheat/rice starter cake carrying Aspergillus and wild yeast) and water, then roughly strained, leaving the solids in suspension.

styles.name: Yakju / Cheongju (약주 / 청주)
styles.impression: The clear, refined liquor drawn off the top of the same ferment — cleaner, stronger and more elegant than makgeolli.
styles.comments: Cheongju is the Korean cousin of sake, though nuruk gives an earthier, more rustic character than koji. Beopju of Gyeongju is a famed example.
styles.ingredients: Rice, nuruk and water; the clear supernatant is decanted (cheongju, 'clear liquor') rather than strained cloudy. Yakju ('medicine liquor') may include botanicals.

styles.name: Jeungnyu-sik Soju (증류식 소주, Traditional Distilled)
styles.impression: Pot-distilled soju from a real grain ferment — rich, grainy and aromatic, the historical drink before dilution soju took over.
styles.comments: A designated regional cultural product. Worlds apart from the cheap green-bottle soju: this is a craft grain spirit, sometimes aged.
styles.ingredients: Rice or other grain fermented with nuruk, then pot-distilled. Andong Soju is the protected regional archetype.

styles.name: Huiseok-sik Soju (희석식 소주, Diluted)
styles.impression: The ubiquitous green-bottle soju: neutral spirit cut with water and sweeteners, clean and near-flavourless by design.
styles.comments: Created as a rice-saving measure; rice-based distilling was banned 1965–1991. Now the best-selling spirit category on earth by bottles.
styles.ingredients: Highly-rectified neutral spirit (from tapioca, rice or other starch) diluted with water, with sweeteners and flavourings added.

styles.name: Bokbunja-ju (복분자주)
styles.impression: Deep-purple Korean black raspberry wine — sweet, tart and fruity, a popular restaurant digestif.
styles.comments: Served at the 2005 APEC summit. Reputed traditionally as a tonic.
styles.ingredients: Korean black raspberry (Rubus coreanus) fermented, sometimes fortified.

styles.name: Munbaeju & Designated Folk Liquors (문배주)
styles.impression: Government-designated Important Intangible Cultural Property liquors — regional recipes preserved by named holders.
styles.comments: Korea protects specific traditional liquors and their makers as living cultural heritage.
styles.ingredients: Varies: Munbaeju is a millet/sorghum distillate scented (despite no pear) of wild pear; Songjeol-ju, Sanseong soju and others each have protected methods.
